**Author:** @infinterenders ("render") · posted 2026-11-09 06:21Z · received 2026-11-09T20:09:11Z (WhatsApp via RDP-30, routed by CoS). 840 likes · 23.5k views · 8 replies at capture (fxtwitter). **First capture from this author** — no verified identity beyond the handle.

**Quoted tweet:** @steveruizok (Steve Ruiz, tldraw founder) — "good prompt 'find all of the implicit state machines in my app'" (posted 2026-11-05, id 2116552016218710389).

## Summary
An elaboration of Ruiz's one-liner into a full recovery prompt for LLM code analysis. The tweet's prompt, verbatim structure:

> "Recover my program's minimal semantic model.
> 1. **State:** every value that changes what the user sees
> 2. **Transitions:** what commutes, what's idempotent, what's order-dependent
> 3. **Dependencies:** what must be true before each effect fires
>
> Then find:
> → nondeterminism in awaits, retries and event order
> → invariants enforced by hope
> → one fact stored in two places, drifting
> → work that never reaches the screen
>
> Last, split my refactors into 'provably equivalent' and 'trust me'. For each 'trust me', give the smallest input that breaks it."

The kicker: **"your app already has a formal semantics. you just haven't met it."** The move is recovery, not specification — don't write the formal model, have the model read it back out of the code.

## Why it matters
- **The vocabulary is the value.** "What commutes / what's idempotent / what's order-dependent" imports concurrency-theory distinctions into a prompt a working engineer will actually run. "Invariants enforced by hope" and "one fact stored in two places, drifting" name two of the oldest failure modes in interactive software (unchecked assumptions, cache/denormalization drift) as first-class search targets.
- **"Provably equivalent" vs "trust me" is the load-bearing part.** It forces the model to *classify its own uncertainty* about refactors instead of blanket-asserting safety — and "give the smallest input that breaks it" turns each trust-me into a checkable counterexample request (property-based-testing instinct applied to review). This is the same leverage as Rauch's proof-checkers thesis: the win comes from making equivalence claims falsifiable.
- **Directly applicable to this company's own stack.** The WhatsApp bridge daemon (wa-bridge.mjs) is exactly the target: retry lanes, await ordering, state files, a media-inbox with dedupe-bytes rules — an implicit state machine that has already produced the Sep/Oct outages. Running this prompt against it is a candidate cheap audit.
- **Third data point in the vault's prompt-craft cluster** (after Ruiz's original and the agrawal simplification prompts): the genre is shifting from "how do I ask nicely" to prompts that impose a *conceptual framework* on the analysis — the prompt is a rubric.
- **Skepticism gates:** the prompt assumes the model can faithfully recover a semantic model from a large codebase — output plausibility ≠ faithfulness, and nothing here mechanically verifies the "provably equivalent" bucket (that label is itself trust-me without a proof checker attached). The elaborate version risks confident prose where Ruiz's terse original forces the model to show its work. Stats are real (840/23.5k) but modest-viral; quote-tweet elaborations ride the parent's audience.
